section.title: Zelophehad's Daughters and Joshua's Appointment
section.sectionRationale: Right after the census confirms a new generation ready for the land, two practical questions surface: what happens to a family's inheritance when there is no son, and who will lead Israel once Moses is gone. Both are answered here, showing that God's justice reaches into inheritance law and that His care for leadership continues without interruption.
section.thesis: When five daughters bring their father's case for an inheritance before Moses, the LORD rules in their favor and establishes a lasting law of inheritance, and in the same chapter Moses, having been told once more that he will not enter the land, asks God to appoint a shepherd for Israel, and Joshua is publicly commissioned to lead.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the daughters of Zelophehad bring their case and the LORD rules in their favor, establishing inheritance law; the LORD tells Moses he will see the land but not enter it, recalling Meribah; and Joshua is publicly commissioned as Moses' successor.

units.label: The daughters of Zelophehad
units.note: why should our father's name disappear

media.alt: Five women standing before Moses and the assembly at the Tent of Meeting
media.caption: Five daughters ask why their father's name should disappear from his clan.

verses.text: Now the daughters of Zelophehad son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, belonged to the clans of Manasseh son of Joseph. These were the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. They approached
the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders, and the whole congregation, and said,
“Our father died in the wilderness, but he was not among the followers of Korah who gathered together against the LORD. Instead, he died because of his own sin, and he had no sons.
Why should the name of our father disappear from his clan because he had no sons? Give us property among our father's brothers.”
So Moses brought their case before the LORD,
and the LORD answered him,
“The daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly. You certainly must give them property as an {{inheritance|inheritance}} among their father's brothers, and transfer their father's inheritance to them.
Furthermore, you shall say to the Israelites, ‘If a man dies and leaves no son, you are to transfer his inheritance to his daughter.
If he has no daughter, give his inheritance to his brothers.
If he has no brothers, give his inheritance to his father's brothers.

And if his father has no brothers, give his inheritance to the next of kin from his clan, that he may take possession of it. This is to be a statutory ordinance for the Israelites, as the LORD has commanded Moses.’”

units.label: Moses told he will see, but not enter, the land

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go up this mountain of the Abarim range and see the land that I have given the Israelites.
After you have seen it, you too will be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was;

for when the congregation contended in the Wilderness of Zin, both of you rebelled against My command to show My holiness in their sight regarding the waters.” Those were the waters of Meribah in Kadesh, in the Wilderness of Zin.

units.label: Joshua commissioned
units.note: a man with the Spirit in him

verses.text: So Moses appealed to the LORD,
“May the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation
who will go out and come in before them, and who will lead them out and bring them in, so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd.”
And the LORD replied to Moses, “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the {{spirit|Spirit}} in him, and lay your hands on him.
Have him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and commission him in their sight.
Confer on him some of your authority, so that the whole congregation of Israel will obey him.

He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who will seek counsel for him before the LORD by the judgment of the Urim. At his command, he and all the Israelites with him, the entire congregation, will go out and come in.”
Moses did as the LORD had commanded him. He took Joshua, had him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation,
and laid his hands on him and commissioned him, as the LORD had instructed through Moses.

inheritance.gloss: Inheritance, a possession passed down within a family. God's ruling in favor of Zelophehad's daughters extends nachalah beyond the expected male line, showing that the LORD's justice actively protects those who would otherwise be overlooked by ordinary custom.

spirit.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Joshua is described as a man with the ruach already in him, marking him as already equipped by God for leadership even before Moses' public commissioning confirms it before the whole congregation.

basic.context: Five sisters, whose father died leaving no sons, bring a bold and unprecedented legal question to Moses: why should their father's inheritance simply vanish because he had no male heir? God rules in their favor and establishes a lasting inheritance law. In the same chapter, Moses, reminded again that he will not enter the land, prays for a successor, and Joshua is publicly commissioned to lead.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history with real legal and pastoral weight: a specific family's situation becomes the occasion for a permanent statute protecting daughters' inheritance rights, and a real leadership transition is handled with public accountability rather than private arrangement.
basic.originalLanguages: The daughters ask that their father's nachalah, inheritance, not disappear, and God rules that it be transferred to them directly, establishing a statute that protects family land even without a son. Joshua is described as already having ruach, spirit, within him, God's prior equipping preceding his public commissioning before the whole congregation.
basic.typology: Moses' prayer that Israel not be like sheep without a shepherd, and God's provision of Joshua, anticipates the New Testament's repeated concern for shepherdless people, most fully answered in Jesus, who calls Himself the good shepherd who will never leave His flock without care, John 10:11.
basic.christ: Moses' plea for a shepherd for God's people, and God's answer in Joshua, whose Hebrew name, Yehoshua, is the same name borne by Jesus, anticipates the true and greater shepherd-leader who brings God's people fully into their rest, something even Joshua's conquest, real as it was, could not finally accomplish, Hebrews 4:8-9.
basic.god: God is scrupulously just, ruling in favor of five women with no legal standing under ordinary custom, and He is also faithfully provident, ensuring Israel is never left without a shepherd even as Moses' own leadership comes to its appointed end.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 36:1-12 revisits and refines this same inheritance law later in the book. Matthew 9:36 pictures Jesus moved with compassion for crowds like sheep without a shepherd, echoing Moses' own words here. Hebrews 4:8-9 notes that Joshua's conquest, however real, did not give the final rest God still promises His people.
basic.oneStory: God's justice reaches even into the overlooked corners of inheritance law, and His care for His people's leadership never lapses, even at the moment of Moses' own passing. Both threads, justice for the vulnerable and unbroken shepherding care, run through the whole Bible and converge fully in Jesus, whose very name Joshua bears, the true shepherd who brings God's people into everlasting inheritance.

context.literary:
The chapter has two halves that look unrelated until they are read together. Verses 1 to 11 are a legal case: a petition, verses 1 to 4, a referral to God, verse 5, a verdict, verse 7, and a general law, verses 8 to 11. Verses 12 to 23 are a leadership transition: God's word about Moses' death, verses 12 to 14, Moses' prayer, verses 15 to 17, God's answer, verses 18 to 21, and Moses' obedience, verses 22 to 23. Both halves ask the same question. When a man dies, what happens to what God gave him? Zelophehad's land passes to his daughters. Moses' charge passes, not to one of his sons, but to Joshua.

The daughters' speech is a small masterpiece of argument. They establish their standing by naming their line back to Joseph, verse 1. They come to the right place, the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, before the right people, verse 2. They anticipate an objection: their father was not one of Korah's rebels, whose households were destroyed, but died 'because of his own sin,' like the rest of his generation, verse 3. Then they frame the issue not as a claim for themselves but for their father's name, verse 4.

The case belongs to a small group in the Torah where Moses has no ready answer and must wait for God: the blasphemer, Leviticus 24:12, the men unclean at Passover, Numbers 9:8, the Sabbath breaker, Numbers 15:34, and here. In each the law grows out of a real situation. This one is unusual because it ends in favour of the petitioners and because the case is reopened in Numbers 36, so the book closes with these five women.

The second half contains no protest from Moses. Where Deuteronomy 3:23 to 26 records him pleading to cross over, here he hears his sentence and at once prays for the people. The chapter ends with a double note of obedience, 'Moses did as the LORD had commanded him,' verse 22, the very thing verse 14 says he failed to do at Meribah.
context.historical:
The setting is the plains of Moab late in the fortieth year. The census has just been taken, and in it Zelophehad's family is singled out, Numbers 26:33. The daughters' question was therefore urgent and practical. The land was about to be divided 'according to the number of names,' Numbers 26:53, and a household with no male name risked being left off the map.

In Israel land was not a commodity but a family trust from God. Naboth's reply to Ahab shows the attitude: 'The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers,' 1 Kings 21:3. Keeping a dead man's name alive on his land was a serious concern, which is why the law of levirate marriage existed, 'so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel,' Deuteronomy 25:6, and why Boaz redeemed Ruth 'to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance,' Ruth 4:10. Zelophehad's daughters use exactly that concern to argue their case.

Practice across the ancient Near East varied, and daughters could sometimes receive property. What stands out here is that the ruling comes directly from the LORD and is made 'a statutory ordinance for the Israelites,' verse 11, with a full order of succession: son, daughter, brothers, father's brothers, nearest kinsman. It was applied in Joshua 17:3 to 6, and one of the five names, Tirzah, is also the name of a Canaanite city, Joshua 12:24, that later served as a royal capital of the northern kingdom, 1 Kings 15:33.

Moses was one hundred and twenty years old, Deuteronomy 31:2. The Abarim range rises east of the Dead Sea above the plains of Moab; Deuteronomy 32:49 locates Mount Nebo within it, and the BSB footnote notes that the Greek translation reads Nebo here. Joshua was no stranger to leadership. He had fought Amalek, Exodus 17:9 to 10, served as Moses' attendant on the mountain, Exodus 24:13, stayed at the tent of meeting, Exodus 33:11, and stood with Caleb against the bad report, Numbers 14:6 to 9. The Urim, literally 'the Lights,' were kept in the high priest's breastpiece, Exodus 28:30, and used to seek God's decision.
context.canonical:
The daughters' case runs through the rest of the Old Testament. Numbers 36 raises a follow up question from their tribe, whether their land would pass to another tribe if they married outside it, and the answer keeps the inheritance within Manasseh while leaving them free to marry 'anyone they please' within their father's tribe, Numbers 36:6. Joshua 17:3 to 4 records the daughters reminding Eleazar and Joshua, 'The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers,' and receiving it. The Chronicler still remembers 'Zelophehad, who had only daughters,' 1 Chronicles 7:15. Job's restored daughters receive an inheritance among their brothers, Job 42:15, a quiet echo of the principle.

The commissioning of Joshua is repeated and developed in Deuteronomy. Moses charges him, 'Be strong and courageous,' Deuteronomy 31:7 to 8, and the LORD Himself commissions him, Deuteronomy 31:23. Deuteronomy 34:9 says Joshua was 'filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him,' and Joshua 1:1 to 6 opens the next book with God's own promise, 'As I was with Moses, so will I be with you.'

Moses' image of sheep without a shepherd becomes a prophetic theme. Micaiah sees Israel 'scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd,' 1 Kings 22:17. Ezekiel 34 indicts Israel's leaders because the flock 'were scattered for lack of a shepherd,' Ezekiel 34:5, and promises 'one shepherd, My servant David,' Ezekiel 34:23. Zechariah 13:7 speaks of the Shepherd struck and the sheep scattered.

In the New Testament Jesus looks on the crowds 'like sheep without a shepherd,' Matthew 9:36 and Mark 6:34, calls Himself the good shepherd, John 10:11, and uses the language of verse 17 when He says His sheep 'will come in and go out and find pasture,' John 10:9. The laying on of hands to set someone apart continues in Acts 6:6 and 13:3 and 1 Timothy 4:14. Hebrews 4:8 names Joshua directly and says his leadership did not bring the final rest.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wanted the new generation, about to receive the land, to understand two things before the first boundary was drawn.

First, that God's law protects the household that ordinary rules might erase. The first hearers would have known families like Zelophehad's. The ruling told them that God Himself had considered such cases and that no Israelite name was to be lost merely because a father had no sons. It also commended a certain kind of faith. The daughters did not seize land or complain in private; they brought their case openly to God's appointed place and trusted Him to answer. The phrase 'speak correctly,' verse 7, is God's commendation of that faith.

Second, that Israel's future did not depend on Moses. The man who had led them for forty years would die on a mountain. The people were meant to see that God had already provided a successor, publicly commissioned, filled with the Spirit and placed under the priest's inquiry of God, so that no one could claim the leadership by force or by rumour. The first hearers were meant to follow Joshua because God had appointed him, and to follow him as a man under God's word, not as a new Moses.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The inheritance ruling of verses 8 to 11 is prescriptive law for Israel, called 'a statutory ordinance,' verse 11, and it governed the allotment in Joshua 17. It is not a code for modern estates, but it shows the kind of justice God cares about: provision for those whom a system might overlook, and a concern for households, names and continuity.

The commissioning of Joshua is narrative about a unique succession. It does not set out a required procedure for choosing leaders today. Yet some elements are taken up in the New Testament: public recognition before the congregation, prayer, and the laying on of hands, Acts 6:6 and 1 Timothy 4:14. The underlying principles carry forward directly. Leaders are to be men whom God has equipped, verse 18, recognised openly, verse 19, accountable to God's word, verse 21, and concerned above all that God's people not be left as sheep without a shepherd. Hebrews 13:17 still speaks of leaders who watch over souls 'as those who must give an account.'

debates.question: Why does God rule so decisively in favor of the daughters when no prior law addressed their situation?

views.label: God's justice actively extends beyond existing custom to protect the vulnerable
views.case: The daughters had no written statute to appeal to, yet God answers 'the daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly,' verse 7. This fits God's character as 'a defender of the widows' and father of the fatherless, Psalm 68:5, and as the one who 'executes justice for the fatherless and widow,' Deuteronomy 10:18. The ruling fills a gap that custom would have left.

views.label: The case shows law developing through real situations under God's guidance
views.case: Several Torah laws arise from specific cases brought to Moses, Leviticus 24:12, Numbers 9:8 and 15:34. God's law is not arbitrary but applied to real circumstances as Israel's life required. The later refinement in Numbers 36 shows the same process continuing when a new question arose.

debates.bearing: The two views fit together. God's justice is not merely theoretical; it responds to cases brought before Him. The ruling both protects a vulnerable household and preserves the larger purpose of the land, keeping each family's name on its inheritance.

debates.question: What was the 'own sin' for which Zelophehad died?

views.label: The sin of his generation
views.case: The simplest reading is that Zelophehad shared in the unbelief at Kadesh and died under the sentence of Numbers 14:29, like every man counted in the first census. The daughters distinguish that ordinary death from the special judgment on Korah's company, whose households perished with them, Numbers 16:32, and so suggest their father's line had not been forfeited.

views.label: A particular sin known to the community
views.case: One strand of Jewish tradition identified Zelophehad with the man gathering wood on the Sabbath, Numbers 15:32, since both belong to the wilderness years. The text gives no support for this, and it goes beyond what Numbers says.

debates.bearing: The text is content to leave the sin general. The point of verse 3 is legal and pastoral: Zelophehad died as a sinner among sinners, not as a rebel whose house was cut off, so his daughters could still receive his inheritance. That is a quiet word of hope for every family whose parents died under the common judgment on sin.

debates.question: Did the laying on of hands give Joshua the Spirit, or recognise a Spirit he already had?

views.label: It recognised and displayed an existing gift
views.case: Verse 18 calls Joshua 'a man with the Spirit in him' before Moses lays a hand on him. The ceremony therefore confirms publicly what God has already done, and 'some of your authority,' verse 20, concerns the people's obedience rather than the Spirit.

views.label: It conveyed a further endowment for the task
views.case: Deuteronomy 34:9 says that Joshua 'was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him.' On this reading the laying on of hands was the means by which God added a fuller gift of wisdom for leadership, much as Paul speaks of the gift in Timothy 'through the laying on of my hands,' 2 Timothy 1:6.

debates.bearing: Both texts are true together. God had already equipped Joshua, and at his commissioning God granted further wisdom for the task. The ceremony is not magic; it is God's chosen occasion for confirming and strengthening the gift He has given.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond nachalah and ruach, several words and phrases give this chapter its texture.

God's verdict in verse 7 opens with a single word, ken, 'correctly' or 'right,' placed first for emphasis: 'Right, the daughters of Zelophehad are speaking.' It is a word of plain approval. Numbers 36:5 uses the same word when God approves the concern raised by the men of Manasseh, so that both sides of the later dispute are said to speak rightly.

The verb 'transfer' in verses 7 and 8 is the causative stem of avar, to cross or pass over: 'you are to cause his inheritance to pass over to his daughter.' The same root runs through the second half of the chapter. The Abarim range of verse 12 takes its name from avar, the mountains of the 'regions beyond' or 'crossings.' And the root is the one used when Moses is told he will not cross, 'You shall not cross the Jordan,' Deuteronomy 31:2. The inheritance crosses over to five daughters, while Moses stands on the mountains of crossing and sees a land he cannot cross into.

Moses addresses God in verse 16 as 'the God of the spirits of all flesh,' elohei haruchot lekol basar. It is the same title Moses and Aaron used in Numbers 16:22 when they pleaded for the congregation during Korah's rebellion. The title confesses that God gives life and breath to every person and knows each one inwardly, which is why Moses trusts Him to choose the right man. Hebrews 12:9 speaks of God as 'the Father of our spirits.'

'Go out and come in' and 'lead them out and bring them in,' verse 17, pair the verbs yatsa and bo. The phrase is used of military leadership, as when David was 'leading them out to battle and back,' 1 Samuel 18:16, and Caleb says his strength is still the same 'for going out, and for coming in,' Joshua 14:11. Moses asks for a leader who will do in battle what he, at a hundred and twenty, can no longer do, Deuteronomy 31:2.

'Lay your hands on him,' verse 18, uses samak, to lean or press. It is the verb of the worshipper laying his hand on the head of the burnt offering, Leviticus 1:4, and of Israel laying hands on the Levites, Numbers 8:10. In each case the act identifies one party with another before God.

'Some of your authority,' verse 20, is literally 'from your splendour,' hod, a word often used of royal and divine majesty, as when God is 'clothed with splendor and majesty,' Psalm 104:1. The preposition matters: Joshua receives a share of Moses' honour, not the whole. He will seek God's will through Eleazar and the Urim, verse 21, whereas God spoke with Moses 'face to face,' Numbers 12:8. The successor is real but not a second Moses.

typology.type: Joshua, the successor who leads the people in and out
typology.fulfillment: Joshua's name was given by Moses, Numbers 13:16, and in Greek it is the same name as Jesus, as Hebrews 4:8 and Acts 7:45 show. Jesus is given His name 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21. Joshua led Israel out to battle and brought them into the land; Jesus says His sheep 'will come in and go out and find pasture,' John 10:9. The escalation lies in what is won: Joshua gave land, Jesus gives 'a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9. The type falls short because Joshua died and left Israel with its enemies still in the land.

typology.type: The shepherd provided so the flock is not scattered
typology.fulfillment: Moses' prayer that the congregation not be 'like sheep without a shepherd' echoes through the prophets, who promise that God Himself will raise one shepherd, Ezekiel 34:23. Jesus sees the crowds in exactly that state and has compassion on them, Mark 6:34, then declares, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:14. The fulfilment exceeds the type, because Joshua led for a lifetime but Jesus lays down His life for the sheep and gives them eternal life so that 'they will never perish,' John 10:28. He is 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20.

typology.type: Daughters who receive their father's inheritance
typology.fulfillment: Five women without a male heir are made heirs by God's own word. The New Testament extends that grace to all who believe: 'You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:26, and 'heirs according to the promise,' Galatians 3:29. Wives are 'fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life,' 1 Peter 3:7. The escalation is that in Christ no one inherits by birth order or gender but by union with the one true Heir. The type falls short because the daughters received land that could be lost; believers receive an inheritance kept in heaven.

typology.type: Moses seeing the land he cannot enter
typology.fulfillment: Moses, the giver of the law, brings Israel to the border but may not bring them in, verse 12 to 14. John writes that 'the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17. The law could lead God's people to the edge of the promise but not across it. The type is completed strikingly on the mount of transfiguration, where Moses stands in glory within the land at last, speaking with Jesus about His 'departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:30 to 31. What Moses could not enter by the law, he enters through Christ.

study.christ:
The clearest link between this chapter and Christ is a name. Moses gave Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua, Numbers 13:16, and in Greek that name is Iesous, Jesus. The New Testament uses it for Joshua himself in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8. When the angel tells Joseph, 'you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21, the name carries the memory of the man commissioned in Numbers 27 to lead God's people into their inheritance.

The chapter also shapes the way Jesus speaks about Himself. Moses prayed for a man 'who will go out and come in before them, and who will lead them out and bring them in, so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd,' verse 17. The Gospels say twice that Jesus looked on the crowds and saw them 'like sheep without a shepherd,' Matthew 9:36 and Mark 6:34, and in Mark He answers by teaching them and feeding them. In John 10 He calls Himself the good shepherd and says of those who enter through Him that they 'will come in and go out and find pasture,' John 10:9. The language of Moses' prayer becomes the language of Jesus' promise.

There is escalation at every point. Joshua had the Spirit in him, verse 18; the One God sent is given 'the Spirit without limit,' John 3:34. Joshua received only some of Moses' splendour, verse 20; Hebrews says that Moses was faithful 'as a servant in all God's house,' but Christ 'as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:5 to 6. Joshua had to ask God's will through a priest and the Urim, verse 21; Jesus is Himself the high priest and speaks the words of God. Joshua gave Israel the land but not the final rest, and so 'There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9.

The first half of the chapter leads to Christ in a different way. Five daughters approach God's presence with a request that custom might have refused, and God says they speak rightly. Jesus welcomed women whom others overlooked, calling a crippled woman 'this daughter of Abraham,' Luke 13:16. More deeply, in Him the inheritance is opened to all who believe, sons and daughters alike, Galatians 3:26 to 29.

The typology should not be pushed beyond its limits. Joshua's conquest was real warfare, and it is not a picture of evangelism. The link to Christ runs through the Bible's own threads: the shared name, the shepherd who leads in and out, and the rest that Joshua could not give.
study.god:
This chapter reveals a God who listens. Five women with no legal precedent come to the door of His tent, and He hears them, weighs their case and rules in their favour. God is not so bound by custom that He cannot see an injustice, and He is not so distant that the concerns of one family escape Him. Psalm 68:5 calls Him 'a father of the fatherless,' and in this chapter He acts like one for the daughters of a man who died in the wilderness.

It shows a God whose justice becomes law. He does not merely make an exception for one family; He writes a rule for all Israel, verses 8 to 11. His care for the vulnerable is not occasional kindness but settled policy, built into the order of His people's life.

It shows a God who is holy even toward His closest servant. Verses 13 and 14 remind Moses why he will not enter: at Meribah he failed 'to show My holiness in their sight.' God does not pretend Moses' sin did not happen. Yet He lets Moses see the land, calls his death a gathering to his people, as with Aaron and Abraham, Genesis 25:8, and allows him to prepare his successor. Discipline and tenderness are held together.

It shows a God who knows the inner life of every person. Moses appeals to 'the God of the spirits of all flesh,' verse 16, and God answers by naming a man in whom the Spirit already dwells. The choice of leaders is not left to lot or ambition. The God who gives breath to all flesh knows whom He has prepared.

And it shows a God who never leaves His people without a shepherd. Leaders die, but the Lord of the flock remains. The same promise is made to Joshua in Deuteronomy 31:8 and Joshua 1:5, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you,' and it rests finally on Jesus' own promise to be with His people 'always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20.

For worship this means we may come to God with our cases as the daughters did, openly and in faith, and we may face the loss of trusted leaders without despair. The Shepherd of Israel still provides.

crossReferences.note: The heads of Manasseh ask whether the daughters' land will pass to another tribe if they marry outside it. God answers that they may marry 'anyone they please' within their father's tribe, so the inheritance stays in Manasseh. The book of Numbers ends by returning to these five women, and they obey.

The ruling is applied. The daughters remind Eleazar and Joshua, 'The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers,' and receive it. The man commissioned in Numbers 27 carries out the law announced in the same chapter, and 'the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance among his sons.'

Boaz marries Ruth 'to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers.' The concern the daughters voiced in Numbers 27:4, that their father's name not disappear, is the same concern that drives the story of Ruth toward David.

Moses and Aaron first use the title 'the God of the spirits of all flesh' when they plead for the congregation during Korah's rebellion. In Numbers 27:16 Moses uses it again to ask God to choose a leader. Both prayers appeal to God's knowledge of every person.

Moses recalls pleading, 'Please let me cross over and see the good land,' and God refusing and telling him to look from the top of Pisgah. Numbers 27 records no such plea, only Moses' prayer for the people, showing the selflessness of his response.

After Moses' death, Joshua 'was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. So the Israelites obeyed him.' The commissioning of Numbers 27:18 to 20 bears the fruit it was meant to have: a Spirit-filled leader and a people who follow.

Micaiah sees 'all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd,' the fate Moses prayed to prevent. The prophet uses Moses' own image to announce the death of a king who led Israel into a battle God had not sent them to fight.

God indicts Israel's leaders because the flock 'were scattered for lack of a shepherd' and became food for wild beasts. The prayer of Numbers 27:17 becomes a charge against failed shepherds and leads to God's promise to shepherd His people Himself through 'My servant David,' Ezekiel 34:23.

Jesus sees a large crowd and has compassion on them 'because they were like sheep without a shepherd.' He teaches them and then feeds them in the wilderness. Moses' phrase is fulfilled not by a better Joshua but by the Shepherd Himself providing for His flock.

Jesus says whoever enters through Him 'will come in and go out and find pasture,' echoing the language of Moses' prayer in Numbers 27:17, and calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. The leader Moses asked for is given in a form beyond anything Moses imagined.

'If Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.' Hebrews honours Joshua's achievement but insists it was not the end. 'There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' which only the greater Joshua gives.

Paul says all who believe are 'sons of God through faith,' that there is 'neither... male nor female' in Christ, and that all who belong to Him are 'heirs according to the promise.' The daughters of Zelophehad received a share by God's ruling; in Christ every believer receives the inheritance by grace.

study.oneStory:
In the story of creation, fall, redemption and new creation, this chapter speaks to two losses caused by the fall: the loss of a name through death, and the loss of a leader through death. From the beginning God gave humanity the earth as an inheritance and blessed it to be fruitful, Genesis 1:28. After the fall death threatened to erase families and cut every human work short. Zelophehad died in the wilderness with no son. Moses, the greatest leader Israel ever had, would die on a mountain outside the land.

Against both losses God acts. He preserves Zelophehad's name by giving his land to his daughters, and He preserves Israel's future by appointing Joshua. The chapter answers the anxious question of the wilderness years: what happens to God's people when the generation of Sinai is gone? God has already provided.

It sets up much of what follows. Joshua will lead Israel across the Jordan and apportion the land, and the daughters will receive their share, Joshua 17:3 to 6. The concern for keeping a name on its inheritance will drive the book of Ruth, which ends with the birth of David's grandfather. The image of sheep without a shepherd will haunt Israel's history, until the prophets promise that God Himself will shepherd His flock through a son of David.

The story reaches its centre in Jesus, whose very name is Joshua. He is the Shepherd who leads His sheep in and out, and who lays down His life for them. He is the Son over God's house, greater than Moses, and He brings His people into a rest that Joshua could not give. In Him the inheritance, once tied to sons and land, is opened to all who believe, daughters and sons alike.

The story ends in a new creation where no name will be lost and no leader will die. The meek will inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, and the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd and guide them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The Shepherd Moses prayed for will never be taken from His flock.

questions: Zelophehad's daughters boldly brought a case for which there was no existing precedent. Where might you need similar courage to bring an honest need before God rather than assuming there is no answer for it?

God ruled decisively in favor of five women with no legal standing under ordinary custom. Where have you seen, or where do you need to trust, God's justice reaching people that human systems tend to overlook?

Moses, even while being told again that he would not enter the land, still prayed for Israel's future leadership rather than his own vindication. Where might God be asking you to care for what comes after you rather than fighting for your own outcome?
Joshua already carried the Spirit before he was publicly commissioned. Where might God already be equipping you for something before the moment it becomes visible to others?

Moses feared Israel being like sheep without a shepherd, and God provided one immediately. Where do you need to trust that Jesus, the good shepherd, is providing exactly the care and direction you feel is missing right now?

translationNotes.note: The full genealogy given for Zelophehad, tracing five generations back to Manasseh, underscores the legal seriousness of the daughters' claim, establishing their standing within the tribe beyond any doubt.

The waters of Meribah in Kadesh is repeated here almost verbatim from Numbers 20:13, showing the author deliberately recalling that earlier failure as the reason for Moses' exclusion, rather than treating it as a new or separate offense.

A man with the Spirit in him, ruach, likely refers to God-given wisdom, discernment, and courage for leadership, the same quality noted of Joshua earlier in Deuteronomy 34:9, rather than a specific miraculous endowment distinct from his established character.
